U.S. refiners rebuild depleted fuel stocks

By processing crude oil at unprecedented rates into the late autumn, U.S. petroleum refiners have rebuilt inventories of gasoline and other fuels badly depleted earlier in the year as a result of the war with Iran. 

Total stocks of gasoline, diesel, jet fuel and other products soared by 13 million barrels over the two weeks ending on November 13, according to data published by the U.S. Energy Information Administration.  

The seasonal accumulation was the largest for more than two decades and contrasted with an average seasonal draw of 10 million barrels in the previous ten years ...

Copper inventories: US stock concentration highlights potential shift towards China
Copper inventories monitored by the three major futures exchanges rose for a third consecutive week, increasing by 5,234 tonnes to 1.093 million tonnes. The modest overall build, however, masks a continued geographical imbalance, with US warehouses holding the overwhelming majority of exchange-monitored stocks.

LME inventories rose by 2,925 tonnes to 332,025, but this increase was entirely driven by an 8,550-tonne build at US warehouses to 249,200 tonnes. Excluding the US, LME inventories would have fallen by 5,625 tonnes, highlighting continued tightness elsewhere. Meanwhile, CME inventories recorded a second consecutive weekly decline, partly offsetting small increases in London and Shanghai.

Despite the recent reductions, CME warehouses still account for an elevated 67% of combined exchange inventories. Including copper held in LME-approved US warehouses lifts the US share to approximately 90%, underscoring the substantial concentration of available exchange stocks in a single market.

The concentration reflects the tariff-driven stockpiling of copper in the US over the past two years, but recent developments suggest these flows may now - but only partly - be starting to reverse. An acute shortage of deliverable copper in China has triggered a historic squeeze in nearby Shanghai futures, while the Yangshan import premium has surged to a record USD 500 per tonne. According to recent reports, traders have begun booking shipments of copper from the US to China, initially involving relatively modest volumes of tens of thousands of tonnes.

With the COMEX premium over LME copper having largely disappeared amid reduced expectations of US import tariffs, the incentive to keep metal in the US has weakened. A part reversal in trade flows could help ease China's physical supply squeeze while reducing the unusually large US inventory overhang. However, the timing and scale will depend on whether Chinese premiums remain sufficiently elevated to cover shipping costs and compensate traders for the risk of renewed US tariff measures.

The Bloomberg Commodity Total Return Index is heading for a fifth consecutive weekly decline, falling 4.4% and extending its cumulative loss over the period to 11.4%, reducing the year-to-date gain to 20%. Beyond higher yields and expectations of further Fed rate hikes hurting global growth prospects, the broad-based selloff may also reflect tightening global dollar liquidity. Rising AI-related financing needs, IPO activity, equity market volatility and elevated energy security costs are boosting demand for cash just as higher interest rates make funding more expensive.

Precious and industrial metals have borne the brunt of the rout, with the AI-driven equity selloff triggering double-digit weekly losses in silver and platinum, while copper has slumped 9.5% to an eight-month low. Gold, despite its safe-haven status, has also been caught in the broader dash for cash, falling 8% as investors liquidate highly liquid assets to meet funding needs, cover losses elsewhere and reduce overall risk exposure.

The energy sector is down 4% on the week, with Brent settling into a narrow range in the low USD 90s amid alternating focus on rising supply from the Middle East and the risk of flare-ups. From an inflation perspective, the more encouraging development has been the sharper decline in distillate fuel prices, with London gasoil down 8% on the week to USD 158 per barrel, compared with around USD 200 at the start of the month. Meanwhile, agriculture is down around 2.5%, weighed down primarily by the stronger dollar and broader risk aversion.
